g10-economics-ue4-t1.overview: A perfectly competitive market is one in which no buyer or seller has any power over price, so every participant is a price taker. This lesson defines the market, lists its characteristics and explains the firm's horizontal demand curve and its revenue.
objectives: Define a perfectly competitive market
Review the characteristics of a perfectly competitive market
Explain the nature of the demand curve facing a firm in a perfectly competitive market
Explain why the firm's demand curve is also its average revenue curve
Calculate total, average and marginal revenue
g10-economics-ue4-t1.simple: In a perfectly competitive market there are so many buyers and sellers that no single one can influence the price; every participant is a price taker. The products are identical, or homogenous, like maize, wheat or salt, so buyers cannot tell which firm produced them. Firms enter and leave the market freely because there are no barriers. Everyone has perfect information about prices and product quality, and firms aim to maximize profit. Because each firm is small relative to the market, it faces a horizontal demand curve drawn at the market price and can sell any quantity at that price. Its total revenue equals price times quantity, and in this market average revenue, marginal revenue and price are all equal.
g10-economics-ue4-t1.detailed:
What perfect competition is. In microeconomics, perfect competition describes a market in which a buyer or seller has no market power, so all buyers and sellers are price takers. It is this distinction that separates perfectly competitive markets from imperfectly competitive ones. In short, no single firm has any influence on the price of the product it sells. Think of a farmers market where each seller offers the same product, such as maize: there is little differentiation between the products and all are sold at an equal price, while sellers and buyers join the market freely without any barrier.

Large numbers and homogenous products. A perfectly competitive market is composed of a large number of buyers and sellers, so the decision of a single buyer or seller cannot affect the price of the commodity; each one is too small in relation to the market. At the same time, products supplied by different firms are identical or homogenous: salt supplied by two sellers, for example, is identical to the extent that buyers cannot tell which firm supplied which unit. In the wheat market there are thousands of farmers selling wheat and millions of consumers using it, so no single buyer or seller can influence the price. Together, these two assumptions make the individual firm a price taker.

Free entry and exit. A new firm has the freedom to produce and supply the product, and an existing firm that believes it is not worth staying in the business can leave the market. There is no barrier that restricts entry into or exit out of a perfectly competitive market.

Perfect information and the profit aim. Both sellers and buyers are assumed to have complete knowledge of the market: every buyer and seller knows the product quality and its nature, current and future prices, and input prices. The objective of firms in perfect competition is profit maximization; firms try to increase revenue and minimize costs so as to increase profit.

The demand curve facing the firm. Because the firm is a price taker, it faces a completely horizontal demand curve for its product, meaning it can sell any amount of output only at the ongoing market price. Once the price is determined by the market, the producer takes the equilibrium price as given, and the firm's demand curve is a horizontal line drawn at that price.

Revenue: total, average and marginal. Revenue is what the firm receives from selling its products. Total revenue (TR) is the total money received from selling a quantity of product, obtained as TR = P x Q, where P is price and Q is quantity sold. Average revenue (AR) is revenue per unit sold, AR = TR/Q = (P x Q)/Q, so AR = P. Average revenue and price have the same meaning, because the seller receives what the purchaser pays: price is the per unit payment made by the buyer and AR is the per unit revenue of the seller. That is why the firm's demand curve and its AR curve are the same line.

Marginal revenue under perfect competition. Marginal revenue (MR) is the change in total revenue resulting from a one unit increase in sales, calculated as the change in TR divided by the change in sales, or MR = TRn - TR(n-1). Since the firm can sell any amount at the given market price, the additional revenue from every extra unit sold is just equal to the market price. Hence in perfect competition AR = MR = P = D, and the AR and MR curves coincide and are horizontal, parallel to the X-axis.

keyTerms.def: A market with many buyers and sellers of an identical product in which no single participant has any influence over price.
A buyer or seller too small relative to the market to influence price, who takes the market price as given.
Products supplied by different firms that are identical, so buyers cannot differentiate which firm supplied which unit.
The absence of barriers preventing new firms from entering or existing firms from leaving a market.
Complete knowledge by all buyers and sellers of product quality, current and future prices, and input prices.
The total money received by a firm from selling its product, TR = P x Q.
Revenue per unit of output sold, AR = TR/Q, which is always equal to price.
The change in total revenue resulting from selling one more unit of the product, MR = TRn - TR(n-1).

workedExamples.problem: A farmer usually sells 100 kg of coffee for Birr 200 per kg. Calculate total revenue and average revenue, and find the marginal revenue of an additional sale at the market price.
workedExamples.given: Quantity sold = 100 kg; price = Birr 200 per kg.
workedExamples.formula: TR = P x Q; AR = TR/Q; in perfect competition MR = P.
workedExamples.calculation: TR = 20,000 Birr; AR = 20,000/100 = 200 Birr per kg. Any additional kg sells at the market price, so its MR equals that price.
workedExamples.answer: TR = 20,000 Birr, AR = 200 Birr per kg; an additional sale earns MR equal to the market price (190 Birr if the price is 190).

workedExamples.problem: A market has thousands of sellers all offering the same grade of maize at the same price. Which market structure is this, and what power does each seller have over price?
workedExamples.given: Many sellers, identical product, one common price, free participation.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: many sellers plus product homogeneity make each firm a price taker.
workedExamples.substitution: No seller's decision can move the market price, and products are not differentiated.
workedExamples.calculation: The characteristics match perfect competition exactly, so the seller must accept the market price.
workedExamples.answer: A perfectly competitive market, and each seller is a price taker with no influence on price.

workedExamples.problem: Compare a wheat farmer with a dealer selling one unique phone brand. Who is more likely to be a price taker, and why?
workedExamples.given: The wheat market has thousands of identical-supply farmers; the phone is a differentiated product with few rivals.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: price-taking follows from large numbers plus homogenous products.
workedExamples.substitution: Wheat is identical across sellers, so buyers switch freely at any small price difference.
workedExamples.calculation: The farmer cannot raise price above the market price without losing all buyers; the phone dealer can charge more for its brand.
workedExamples.answer: The wheat farmer is the price taker; the phone dealer, facing a differentiated product, is not in a perfectly competitive setting.

workedExamples.problem: At a market price of Birr 20, a competitive firm sells 50 units. State TR, AR and MR for this firm and explain why they relate this way.
workedExamples.formula: TR = P x Q; AR = TR/Q; in perfect competition AR = MR = P.
workedExamples.calculation: TR = 1,000 Birr; AR = 20 Birr; each extra unit adds sales revenue equal to the price, so MR = 20 Birr.
workedExamples.answer: TR = 1,000 Birr; AR = MR = P = 20 Birr, because the firm sells any quantity at the fixed market price.

commonMistakes: Thinking an individual seller in perfect competition can raise the price slightly, when in fact buyers would simply buy from others at the market price.
Confusing the horizontal demand curve of the individual firm with the downward-sloping market demand curve of the whole market.
Believing a perfectly competitive firm chooses its own price, when it only chooses the quantity to sell at the given price.
Assuming products must have different brand names in a competitive market, ignoring the requirement of homogeneity.
Forgetting that free entry and exit, not just many sellers, is required for perfect competition.
Thinking marginal revenue is different from price in perfect competition, when AR = MR = P.
Assuming buyers or sellers know little about the market, when perfect information is assumed.
applications: A maize or wheat farmer in Ethiopia checks the daily market price before selling, because no single farmer can set the price.
Traditional grain and vegetable markets, where sellers offer the same produce side by side, work close to the perfectly competitive model.
Recognising that when farmers sell identical coffee at the same price, the market, not the farmer, determines revenue.
Understanding why homogenous products such as salt command one market price rather than seller-specific prices.
Explaining why firms in such markets do not spend on advertising, since products are identical and everyone has perfect information.
g10-economics-ue4-t1.summary: A perfectly competitive market has many buyers and sellers, homogenous products, free entry and exit, perfect information and profit-maximizing firms. Each firm is a price taker facing a horizontal demand curve at the market price, and its AR, MR and demand curves coincide with the price. Total revenue is P x Q, and every extra unit sold adds revenue equal to the market price.

questions.q: In a perfectly competitive market, an individual firm is a:
questions.explanation: Because it is too small relative to the market, the firm takes the market price as given.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a perfectly competitive market?
questions.explanation: A single seller describes monopoly, the opposite of perfect competition.

questions.q: A perfectly competitive firm faces a horizontal demand curve drawn at the market price.
questions.explanation: The firm can sell any amount of output only at the ongoing market price, so its demand curve is horizontal at that price.

questions.q: In a perfectly competitive market, one seller's decision can raise the market price of the commodity.
questions.explanation: The firm is too small in relation to the market, so no single seller can influence the price.

questions.q: In perfect competition, average revenue is always equal to what?
questions.explanation: AR = TR/Q = P, because the seller receives exactly what the buyer pays per unit.

questions.q: Name the characteristic of perfect competition in which buyers are unable to tell which firm supplied which unit of the product.
questions.explanation: Homogeneity of products means the supplies of different firms are identical.

questions.q: A competitive firm sells 30 kg of grain at Birr 150 per kg. What is its total revenue?
questions.explanation: TR = P x Q = 150 x 30 = 4,500 Birr.

questions.q: When a competitive firm's total revenue rises from 600 Birr to 620 Birr as it sells one more unit, its marginal revenue is:
questions.explanation: MR = TRn - TR(n-1) = 620 - 600 = 20 Birr, which equals the market price.

questions.q: Explain why the firm's demand curve and its average revenue curve are the same line.
questions.answer: seller receives what buyer pays|per unit revenue equals per unit price|AR equals price
questions.explanation: Price is the per unit payment by the buyer and AR is the per unit revenue of the seller; since the seller receives what the purchaser pays, the two curves coincide.

questions.q: The assumption that buyers and sellers know current and future prices and product quality is called:
questions.explanation: Perfect information for both consumers and producers is a defining assumption of perfect competition.

questions.q: Arrange the market structures from the largest number of firms to the fewest.
questions.explanation: The order is perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, then monopoly with a single firm.

g10-economics-ue4-t2.overview: A pure monopoly is a market with a single supplier facing no close substitutes, which makes the firm a price maker. This lesson defines monopoly, explains its characteristics and sources, and analyses the monopolist's downward-sloping demand and revenue curves.
objectives: Define a pure monopoly market and trace the Greek origin of the term
Review the characteristic features of pure monopoly
Describe the reasons for the existence of pure monopoly
Analyse the demand curve of a monopoly firm
Analyse the total, average and marginal revenue of a monopoly firm
g10-economics-ue4-t2.simple: The word monopoly comes from the Greek words monos, meaning single, and polus, meaning a seller. A monopoly is a market structure with only one supplier in an industry, and that firm is the price maker while consumers are price takers. The monopolist sells a product with no close substitutes, so buyers have no alternative. Entry is blocked by barriers such as licences, patent rights and economies of scale. Because the monopolist controls total supply, it faces a downward-sloping demand curve and must accept a lower price to sell more. Total revenue first rises, reaches a maximum and then falls, while both average revenue and marginal revenue decline, with marginal revenue always below average revenue.
g10-economics-ue4-t2.detailed:
What pure monopoly is. The term monopoly derives from two Greek words: monos, meaning single, and polus, meaning a seller. A monopoly is a market structure in which there is only one supplier in a given market or industry. For this position to last, sufficient restrictions must prevent any other firm from entering and selling the commodity. When there is only one firm in the market, the firm is the price maker while consumers are price takers. For example, ELPA, which produces and supplies electric power in Ethiopia, can be considered a monopoly firm, although it is state owned.

Single seller, one-firm industry, no substitutes. A pure or absolute monopoly is a one-firm industry that sells to many buyers. The firm has full control over both the supply and the price of the product, and the firm and the industry are one and the same. The monopolist's product has no close substitutes, meaning consumers have no alternative choices and the firm faces no competition from new or existing products; for instance, there is no close substitute for the electric services provided by ELPA.

Price maker and price discrimination. The individual firm exercises considerable control over price because it is responsible for the total quantity supplied. Because its demand curve is downward sloping, the monopolist can influence the market price by changing the quantity it supplies. Under monopoly, price discrimination is also possible: the monopolist can sell its product at different prices to different customers.

Restrictions on entry. New competitors cannot freely enter a monopoly market because of strict barriers. These may be legal restrictions such as licensing or patent rights, or restrictions created by economies of scale. The barriers are what allow the monopolist to maintain its monopoly power.

Why monopolies exist. Several sources sustain monopoly power. First, the absence of close substitutes lets a sole seller enjoy the market. Second, economies of scale: a firm whose long-run average cost is declining can produce very cheaply at large scale; when small firms try to enter, the incumbent produces a large output to minimize unit cost and charges a lower price to deter entry. Third, ownership of strategic or key inputs, such as a raw material a firm refuses to sell to others; Ambo mineral water has monopolized the natural mineral water input. Fourth, patent rights for products or processes, and government policies such as licensing or foreign trade restrictions like quotas, which limit the number of sellers. Finally, a company may develop a unique product or technique and protect it with patent or copy rights; MOHA and Coca Cola have maintained monopoly power over their products partly through exclusive knowledge of the ingredient chemicals required for production.

The demand curve of the monopolist. Unlike the competitive price taker, the monopoly is the sole producer, so it can alter the price of its goods by adjusting the quantity supplied. It therefore faces a downward-sloping market demand curve: if it wants to sell more output it must accept a lower price, and if it raises the price, consumers buy less. The monopolist would prefer a high price with a large quantity, but the demand curve makes that impossible: it can choose any point on the demand curve, but no point off it. Assuming a linear demand curve, it can be written as P = a - bQ, where P is price, Q is quantity demanded, and a and b are positive constants.

Revenue of the monopolist. Total revenue is again TR = P x Q; substituting the demand function gives TR = (a - bQ)Q = aQ - bQ squared, so the TR curve is inverse U shaped: total revenue first increases with sales, reaches a maximum, and finally decreases. Average revenue equals price, so AR = P and the AR curve is the downward-sloping demand curve. Marginal revenue, the extra revenue from one more unit sold (MR = TRn - TR(n-1)), is less than average revenue and also downward sloping. In the textbook table, price falls from 11 to 3 Birr as quantity rises from 0 to 8 units: total revenue climbs from 0 to a maximum of 30 Birr at 5 units, then falls, while marginal revenue declines from 10 to 2, reaches 0 at the 6th unit, and turns negative at -2 and -4 afterwards.

keyTerms.def: A market structure with a single supplier of a product without close substitutes, from the Greek monos (single) and polus (seller).
A firm with considerable control over price because it controls the total quantity supplied; the monopolist fixes its own price.
A condition in which consumers have no alternative product to switch to, so the monopolist faces no competition.
Selling the same product at different prices to different customers, which is possible under monopoly.
Legal restrictions such as licensing and patent rights, or cost advantages such as economies of scale, that block new competitors.
A declining long-run average cost as output expands, allowing a large firm to produce and price below potential entrants.
A legal monopoly right over a product or production process that prevents competitors from copying it.
The change in total revenue from selling one more unit, MR = TRn - TR(n-1), which lies below average revenue in monopoly.

workedExamples.problem: Using the monopoly revenue table, at quantity 4 the price is Birr 7. Compute total, average and marginal revenue at that quantity.
workedExamples.given: Q = 4 units; P = Birr 7; TR at Q = 3 was Birr 24.
workedExamples.formula: TR = P x Q; AR = TR/Q = P; MR = TRn - TR(n-1).
workedExamples.calculation: TR = 28 Birr; AR = 28/4 = 7 Birr; MR = 4 Birr.
workedExamples.answer: TR = 28 Birr, AR = 7 Birr and MR = 4 Birr, showing MR below AR under monopoly.

workedExamples.problem: ELPA is the only producer and supplier of electric power in Ethiopia, and there is no close substitute for electric services. Classify this market and identify the firm's power over price.
workedExamples.given: A single seller, many buyers, a product with no close substitutes, blocked entry.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a one-firm industry with no close substitutes is a pure monopoly.
workedExamples.substitution: The firm controls total supply, so it can influence the market price by changing quantity.
workedExamples.calculation: All the defining conditions of monopoly are met, so the firm is a price maker and consumers are price takers.
workedExamples.answer: It is a pure monopoly, and the firm is a price maker that fixes its own price.

workedExamples.problem: Ambo mineral water controls the natural mineral water source, and MOHA and Coca Cola keep exclusive knowledge of their ingredient chemicals. Identify the source of monopoly power in each case.
workedExamples.given: Case 1 is control of a raw material input; Case 2 is exclusive product knowledge protected from copying.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: monopoly arises from ownership of strategic inputs and from patents or exclusive knowledge.
workedExamples.substitution: In Case 1 rivals cannot obtain the key input; in Case 2 rivals cannot copy the formula.
workedExamples.calculation: Both block entry, one by denying inputs and one by legal or knowledge protection.
workedExamples.answer: Case 1 is ownership of a strategic or key input; Case 2 is exclusive knowledge backed by patent or copy rights.

workedExamples.problem: A monopolist sells 2 units at Birr 9 each. If it raises the price to Birr 10, only 1 unit is bought. What does this reveal about its demand curve, and why can it not sell a large quantity at a high price?
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the monopoly faces a downward-sloping market demand curve.
workedExamples.substitution: A higher price reduces the quantity bought; a lower price increases it.
workedExamples.calculation: The monopolist can choose any point on the demand curve but cannot choose a point off it, so a high price forces low sales.
workedExamples.answer: The demand curve slopes downward; the monopolist must accept a lower price to sell more output.

commonMistakes: Thinking a monopoly means only one buyer, when it means only one seller.
Believing a monopolist can choose both a high price and a large quantity, ignoring the downward-sloping demand curve.
Assuming marginal revenue equals price in monopoly, when MR is always below AR.
Thinking the total revenue of a monopolist rises forever, when it is inverse U shaped and falls after the maximum.
Forgetting that price discrimination is possible under monopoly.
Assuming monopolies exist only because of government, when economies of scale and control of key inputs also create them.
Confusing the monopoly firm with the industry, when in monopoly the firm and the industry are one and the same.
applications: ELPA's electric power supply shows a state-owned monopoly where households take the given price with no alternative supplier.
Ambo mineral water's control of natural mineral water shows how owning a strategic input blocks rivals.
MOHA and Coca Cola's exclusive ingredient formulas show how copy rights protect monopoly power over soft drinks.
Licensing and patent policies show how government decisions can limit the number of sellers in Ethiopian industries.
Understanding why the firm and industry are the same helps explain why one power provider can set tariffs by adjusting supply.
Recognising price discrimination, such as different charges to different customer groups by a sole supplier.
g10-economics-ue4-t2.summary: A pure monopoly is a one-firm industry selling a product without close substitutes, protected by barriers such as licences, patents and economies of scale. Sources of monopoly include the absence of substitutes, economies of scale, ownership of strategic inputs like Ambo's mineral water, and exclusive knowledge as with MOHA and Coca Cola. The monopolist is a price maker facing a downward-sloping demand curve, with TR inverse U shaped and MR always below the declining AR.

steps.label: AR = P
steps.detail: Average revenue equals price and follows the downward-sloping demand curve.

steps.label: MR falls faster
steps.detail: Marginal revenue is always less than average revenue and slopes down too.

steps.label: TR rises
steps.detail: Total revenue increases as sales expand from zero.

steps.label: TR maximum
steps.detail: TR peaks where MR reaches zero, such as 30 Birr at 5 units.

steps.label: TR falls
steps.detail: After the peak, MR turns negative and total revenue declines.

questions.q: The word monopoly is derived from Greek words meaning:
questions.explanation: Monos means single and polus means a seller.

questions.q: Under a pure monopoly, the firm is the price maker and consumers are the price takers.
questions.explanation: With only one supplier controlling supply and price, the firm sets the price while buyers must accept it.

questions.q: Which of the following is a source of monopoly power mentioned in the lesson?
questions.explanation: Owning or controlling the entire supply of a key raw material, like Ambo mineral water, sustains monopoly.

questions.q: What is the term for selling the same product at different prices to different customers?
questions.explanation: Price discrimination is possible under monopoly conditions.

questions.q: Explain why a monopolist must lower its price to sell more output.
questions.answer: downward-sloping demand|higher price means fewer buyers|demand curve slopes down
questions.explanation: The monopoly faces the downward-sloping market demand curve, so more sales are possible only at a lower price.

questions.q: In a monopoly, the total revenue curve is:
questions.explanation: TR first increases with sales, reaches a maximum, and finally decreases as sales rise further.

questions.q: In a monopoly, marginal revenue is greater than average revenue at every level of sales.
questions.explanation: MR is less than AR and both curves slope downward; MR even becomes zero and then negative.

questions.q: Write the linear form of the demand curve assumed for a monopolist.
questions.explanation: The linear demand function is P = a - bQ, where a and b are positive constants.

questions.q: Why does economies of scale help an incumbent firm deter new entrants?
questions.answer: large output lowers unit cost|incumbent charges a lower price|declining average cost
questions.explanation: With declining long-run average cost, the incumbent produces a large output to minimize unit cost and charges a lower price than new firms can match.

questions.q: According to the lesson, a state-owned example of a monopoly firm in Ethiopia is:
questions.explanation: ELPA produces and supplies electric power as the sole supplier, though state owned.

questions.q: Arrange the monopoly revenue events in the order they occur as sales increase.
options: TR falls toward negative MR territory
questions.explanation: TR first rises from zero, then peaks as MR approaches zero; after MR hits zero and turns negative, TR falls.

g10-economics-ue4-t3.overview: A monopolistically competitive market has relatively many sellers offering differentiated products with free entry and exit, so it combines features of competition and monopoly. This lesson defines the market, lists its characteristics and explains its demand and revenue curves.
objectives: Define a monopolistically competitive market
Review the characteristics of monopolistic competition
Explain product differentiation and give examples of differentiated products
Describe non-price competition and its forms
Explain the nature of the demand and revenue curves of a monopolistically competitive firm
g10-economics-ue4-t3.simple: Monopolistic competition is a market with relatively large numbers of sellers and buyers, free entry and exit, and differentiated products. When you enter a stationery shop and choose one pen among many kinds, you are in this market. Each product is at least slightly different in style, brand name or quality, which gives each seller a limited monopoly power over customers who prefer its product. Yet the many firms and free entry keep the market competitive, so the actual situation lies between perfect competition and monopoly, making it a very realistic market. Firms also compete without cutting prices through advertising, quality, brand names and customer service, building brand loyalty. Each firm faces a downward-sloping but relatively flat demand curve, with marginal revenue below average revenue.
g10-economics-ue4-t3.detailed:
What monopolistic competition is. A monopolistic competition market refers to a market structure where there are relatively large numbers of sellers and buyers, and there is free entry and exit of firms producing and selling differentiated, or heterogeneous, products. A seller of a differentiated product has limited monopoly power over customers who prefer his or her product to others. The market has some features of competition and some features of monopoly: it is competitive because of the large number of firms and the absence of entry barriers, while its monopoly features result from the differentiated, close-substitute products. It is therefore the more real market, and its actual situations lie somewhere between a perfectly competitive market and a monopoly market.

Product differentiation. Each firm produces and supplies a product that is at least slightly different from those of other firms. The difference could be in style, brand name, quality or other attributes. Different firms produce products like pens, biscuits and soap; stores sell different styles of clothing; restaurants sell different kinds of food; and even beer may be similar in content yet different in public perception because of advertising and brand names. Differentiation is what lets a firm win and keep its own group of loyal buyers.

Many sellers and buyers; free entry and exit. Monopolistic competition also involves many sellers and buyers of the product, though relatively fewer than in a perfectly competitive market. Like perfect competition, there is no barrier to new firms willing and able to produce and supply the product if they find it profitable, and any firm that believes it is not worth staying in the business is free to exit.

Non-price competition. Because of product differentiation, firms compete in ways other than price, and this non-price competition is an essential part of monopolistic competition. It takes the form of product quality, advertising, brand name and customer service. For example, a firm spends money on advertisements to inform consumers about the relatively unique characteristics of its product, thereby attracting new buyers and developing brand loyalty.

The demand curve. As a result of product differentiation, firms are price makers and each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve, which is not horizontal as in perfect competition. However, the firm has few rivals, whereas a monopoly firm has no rivals at all, so the demand curve of a firm under monopolistic competition is flatter than that of a monopoly firm. It is also not the market demand curve, as in the case of monopoly. In practice, the firm expects demand for its product to increase if it lowers its price.

Revenue. The demand curve of the firm is also its average revenue curve, so the firm has a downward-sloping AR curve. Marginal revenue is less than average revenue, and the MR curve is downward sloping as well, exactly as under monopoly but attached to a flatter demand curve.

keyTerms.def: A market with relatively many sellers and buyers, free entry and exit, and differentiated products; it lies between perfect competition and monopoly.
Making a product at least slightly different from rivals' products in style, brand name, quality or other attributes.
Products that differ slightly across firms, unlike the identical goods of perfect competition.
The small price-setting power a seller holds over customers who prefer its differentiated product.
Competing through product quality, advertising, brand name and customer service instead of cutting price.
Customers' habit of preferring one brand, developed through advertising and perceived uniqueness.
The absence of barriers, so new firms enter when profitable and existing firms leave freely.
The monopolistic competitor's downward-sloping demand curve, less steep than a monopolist's because it has few rivals.

workedExamples.problem: You walk into a stationery shop to buy a pen and find shelves of many different kinds of pens from different makers. What market are you participating in, and why?
workedExamples.given: Many sellers offer pens, but each type or brand is at least slightly different.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: relatively many sellers plus product differentiation, with free entry, define monopolistic competition.
workedExamples.substitution: The products are close substitutes, not identical, so sellers are neither pure price takers nor pure monopolists.
workedExamples.calculation: The characteristics match monopolistic competition, so each seller has limited monopoly power over buyers who prefer its pen.
workedExamples.answer: Monopolistic competition, because there are relatively many sellers of differentiated products with free entry and exit.

workedExamples.problem: Compare a wheat farmer in a large grain market with a biscuit producer selling its own brand. Who has some power over price and why?
workedExamples.given: Wheat is homogenous with thousands of sellers; biscuits differ by brand, quality and taste.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: product differentiation grants limited monopoly power; homogeneity grants none.
workedExamples.substitution: The farmer sells an identical product, so buyers switch at any higher price; the biscuit brand has loyal customers.
workedExamples.calculation: The biscuit producer can charge slightly more without losing all customers, while the farmer cannot.
workedExamples.answer: The biscuit producer has limited price power from brand differentiation; the wheat farmer is a pure price taker.

workedExamples.problem: A restaurant in your town refuses to cut its meal prices but improves food quality, decor and customer service, and advertises locally. What kind of competition is this and what is it trying to build?
workedExamples.given: Competition occurs through quality, service and advertising rather than price.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: non-price competition is an essential part of monopolistic competition.
workedExamples.substitution: Advertising informs consumers of the relatively unique characteristics of the product.
workedExamples.calculation: The strategy aims to attract new buyers and develop brand loyalty instead of winning by lower price.
workedExamples.answer: Non-price competition, intended to win new buyers and build brand loyalty.

workedExamples.problem: Place the demand curves of a wheat farmer, a biscuit maker and a sole electric power supplier in order of steepness, and explain.
workedExamples.given: The farmer is a price taker; the biscuit maker has few rivals; the power supplier is the only seller.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: more substitution rivals mean a flatter demand curve.
workedExamples.substitution: The farmer's demand is horizontal; the biscuit maker slopes down gently; the monopolist slopes down most steeply.
workedExamples.calculation: Perfect competition gives a horizontal curve; monopolistic competition is flatter than monopoly because the firm has few rivals, not none.
workedExamples.answer: From flattest to steepest: wheat farmer (horizontal), biscuit maker, then the monopoly power supplier.

commonMistakes: Assuming monopolistic competition means one firm dominates, when the name refers to differentiated products competing among many firms.
Thinking differentiated products are entirely different goods, when they are close substitutes like pens, biscuits or soap.
Confusing the monopolistic competitor's demand curve with a monopoly's market demand curve, when the firm's curve is flatter and not the market curve.
Believing price cutting is the only way to attract buyers, ignoring non-price competition such as quality and customer service.
Expecting buyers of a brand to switch instantly over a tiny price difference, ignoring brand loyalty.
Assuming entry is blocked as in monopoly, when entry and exit are free.
applications: Town and city restaurants selling different kinds of food, where each competes on taste, service and atmosphere rather than only price.
Stores selling different styles of clothing, where brand and style choices give each shop its loyal customers.
Biscuit, soap and beer producers in Ethiopia advertising to show the unique characteristics of their brands.
Stationery shops offering many kinds of pens, a daily example of differentiated close substitutes.
Understanding why a small shop can charge slightly more for a product customers prefer, yet cannot raise prices far.
Noticing how free entry lets new cafes and shops open whenever existing ones appear profitable.
g10-economics-ue4-t3.summary: Monopolistic competition combines competition and monopoly: relatively many sellers and buyers with free entry and exit, but products differentiated in style, brand name or quality. Differentiation gives each firm limited monopoly power, so it is a price maker facing a downward-sloping but flatter demand curve than a monopolist. Firms also engage in non-price competition through quality, advertising, brand name and customer service, while its AR curve slopes downward with MR below it.

pairs.q: Why does a monopolistically competitive firm have limited monopoly power?
pairs.a: Its differentiated product is preferred by some customers, but close substitutes exist.

pairs.q: How is its demand curve different from a monopolist's?
pairs.a: It is downward sloping but flatter, because the firm has few rivals while a monopolist has none.

pairs.q: Give three forms of non-price competition.
pairs.a: Product quality, advertising and brand name, plus customer service.

pairs.q: Why is this called the more real market?
pairs.a: Its actual situations lie between perfect competition and monopoly.

questions.q: A monopolistically competitive market is one in which firms sell:
options: One single product with no substitute
questions.explanation: Firms produce and sell differentiated, or heterogeneous, products that are close substitutes.

questions.q: There is free entry and exit of firms in a monopolistically competitive market.
questions.explanation: Like perfect competition, new firms can enter freely and existing firms can exit freely.

questions.q: A seller of a differentiated product in monopolistic competition has:
options: Limited monopoly power over customers who prefer the product
questions.explanation: Product differentiation gives the seller limited monopoly power over its preferring customers.

questions.q: Competition through advertising, brand name, quality and customer service rather than price is called:
questions.explanation: Non-price competition is an essential part of monopolistic competition.

questions.q: How does the demand curve of a monopolistically competitive firm compare with a monopolist's?
options: It is steep and equals the market demand curve
It is downward sloping but flatter
questions.explanation: The firm has few rivals while a monopoly has none, so its downward-sloping demand curve is flatter.

questions.q: The marginal revenue curve of a monopolistically competitive firm lies below its average revenue curve.
questions.explanation: The firm has a downward-sloping AR curve, and MR is less than AR and also downward sloping.

questions.q: Explain in one sentence why monopolistic competition is described as combining features of both competition and monopoly.
questions.answer: many firms and free entry are competitive|differentiated products give monopoly power|it lies between the two markets
questions.explanation: Competition comes from many firms and free entry; monopoly features come from product differentiation.

questions.q: Give one example of product differentiation named in the lesson.
questions.explanation: Products differ in style, brand name or quality, as with pens, biscuits, soap, clothing styles, restaurants and beer.

questions.q: A firm advertises the relatively unique characteristics of its product mainly to:
options: Get new buyers and develop brand loyalty
questions.explanation: Advertising in non-price competition attracts new buyers and develops brand loyalty.

questions.q: Arrange the features from the most competitive pole to the most monopolistic pole.
questions.explanation: Homogeneity is the competitive extreme, then differentiated close substitutes, and no substitutes is the monopoly extreme.

g10-economics-ue4-t4.overview: An oligopoly is a market with a few dominant firms whose decisions are mutually interdependent, producing identical or closely substituted products. This lesson defines oligopoly, lists its characteristics, introduces the duopoly and explains its demand and revenue.
objectives: Define the oligopoly market
Review the characteristics of the oligopoly market
Explain why firms in an oligopoly are mutually interdependent
Describe the duopoly as the simplest type of oligopoly
Explain the nature of the demand and revenue functions in an oligopoly
g10-economics-ue4-t4.simple: An oligopoly is a market organization in which only a few firms produce identical or closely substituted products. The number of sellers is more than one but so small that the contribution of each firm is not negligible, so the firms sit in mutual interdependence: one firm's actions directly affect its rivals, and all firms follow one another. Barriers such as economies of scale, large capital requirements, patents, technology or control of raw materials keep new firms out. The world crude oil market, where a few Middle Eastern countries control much of the world's reserves, is an example, and cement and sugar factories are oligopoly firms in Ethiopia. The simplest case is the duopoly, with exactly two firms. Oligopolists are price makers facing downward-sloping demand that shifts whenever rivals change their prices.
g10-economics-ue4-t4.detailed:
What oligopoly is. An oligopoly is a market organization in which there are few firms that produce identical or closely substituted products, either identical or differentiated. An oligopoly is said to exist when there is more than one seller in the market, but their number is not so large as to make the contribution of each firm negligible. Firms are therefore situated in mutual interdependence: each behaves as if one firm's actions are directly affected by those of its rivals and by the actions of others. One example is the world market for crude oil, where a few countries in the Middle East control much of the world's oil reserves; cement and sugar factories are examples of oligopoly firms in Ethiopia.

Few dominant firms and interdependence. The number of firms is small enough that each firm recognizes the actions of the other firms. The decision of one firm affects all firms, and so all firms follow the other firms. This interdependence is the defining behaviour of oligopoly: a firm cannot set its price or output without thinking about how rivals will respond.

Entry barriers. In an oligopoly market, entry is difficult or impossible for new firms. Barriers to entry may arise from economies of scale and large capital requirements, which are greater in oligopoly than in other markets except monopoly. Patents, access to technology, or control of raw materials may also exclude potential competitors.

Duopoly. A duopoly is the simplest type of oligopoly: a special case of oligopoly in which there are only two firms in the industry. The lesson gives Ethio-Telecom and Safaricom Ethiopia as a duopoly example.

Demand of the oligopolist. As a result of product differentiation, firms in an oligopoly are price makers and each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve. However, any change in price by one firm may result in price changes by rival firms, and as a consequence the demand curve faced by an oligopolist firm keeps on shifting.

Revenue. Like in all other markets, the revenues of an oligopolist are the receipts from selling its products. The AR curve of the firm is the same as its demand curve, so the firm has a downward-sloping AR curve, and the marginal revenue curve is less than the average revenue curve. Oligopoly therefore resembles monopoly in revenue shape, but unlike monopoly its demand position is unstable because rivals react.

keyTerms.def: A market with a few firms producing identical or closely substituted products, whose contribution is not negligible.
The situation in which each firm's actions, especially price and output changes, directly affect its rivals, so all firms follow one another.
The simplest type of oligopoly, an industry with exactly two firms, such as Ethio-Telecom and Safaricom Ethiopia.
A condition making entry difficult or impossible for new firms, such as economies of scale, large capital needs, patents or raw material control.
Falling average cost with large-scale output, which gives big incumbent firms a cost advantage over entrants.
The oligopolist's demand curve, which keeps moving because rivals change their prices in response to each other.
Oligopoly products may be homogenous across firms, as in cement, or differentiated close substitutes.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia has a small number of cement factories, and each factory's output covers a noticeable share of national supply. Classify this market and name its key behavioural feature.
workedExamples.given: More than one seller but so few that each firm's contribution is significant.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: few firms whose contribution is not negligible define an oligopoly.
workedExamples.substitution: Each firm recognizes the actions of the others, so one firm's decision affects all firms.
workedExamples.calculation: The market matches oligopoly, dominated by few firms with mutual interdependence.
workedExamples.answer: An oligopoly, and the key feature is mutual interdependence among the firms.

workedExamples.problem: The Ethiopian telecom market has two operators, Ethio-Telecom and Safaricom Ethiopia. Identify the market type and justify it.
workedExamples.given: Exactly two firms supply telecom services in the country.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a duopoly is a special case of oligopoly with only two firms.
workedExamples.substitution: There is more than one seller, but the number is far too small to make any contribution negligible.
workedExamples.calculation: Two firms in the industry is the definition of the simplest oligopoly, the duopoly.
workedExamples.answer: A duopoly, the simplest type of oligopoly, with only two firms.

workedExamples.problem: One oligopoly firm announces a price cut. Predict how rivals respond and what happens to the firm's demand curve.
workedExamples.given: Firms are mutually interdependent; each follows the actions of others.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a price change by one firm may result in price changes by rival firms.
workedExamples.substitution: Rivals may match the cut to defend their customers, changing the price-quantity combinations available to the first firm.
workedExamples.calculation: Because rivals react, the demand curve faced by the oligopolist keeps on shifting rather than staying fixed.
workedExamples.answer: Rivals change their own prices, so the firm's demand curve shifts instead of remaining stable.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the revenue structure of an oligopolist with that of a perfectly competitive firm.
workedExamples.given: An oligopolist is a price maker; a competitive firm is a price taker.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: AR equals the demand curve; in oligopoly AR slopes downward, with MR below AR.
workedExamples.substitution: The competitive firm has AR = MR = P on a horizontal curve; the oligopolist's AR slopes down.
workedExamples.calculation: The oligopolist, like a monopolist, sees MR less than AR and downward sloping.
workedExamples.answer: The competitive firm has AR = MR = horizontal; the oligopolist has a downward-sloping AR with MR below it.

commonMistakes: Assuming an oligopoly is a two-firm market in general, when a duopoly is only its simplest special case.
Ignoring mutual interdependence by predicting a firm's price change without considering rivals' reactions.
Believing entry is as easy as in perfect competition, when large capital requirements and patents block entrants.
Confusing oligopoly with monopoly, since oligopoly has more than one seller.
Assuming oligopoly products must be identical, when they may be identical or differentiated.
Expecting the oligopolist's demand curve to stay fixed, when it shifts as rivals change prices.
Thinking MR equals AR in oligopoly, when MR is below the downward-sloping AR.
applications: Ethio-Telecom and Safaricom Ethiopia in the telecom sector illustrate a duopoly, the simplest oligopoly.
Cement factories in Ethiopia show a few dominant firms each supplying a large share of the market.
Sugar factories in Ethiopia are examples of oligopoly firms among domestic producers.
The world crude oil market, controlled by a few Middle Eastern countries, shows how few sellers influence the global price.
Predicting rivals' price reactions before cutting prices is the practical habit of managers in oligopoly industries.
Understanding why starting a telecom, cement or sugar business requires very large capital explains the sector's high entry barriers.
g10-economics-ue4-t4.summary: An oligopoly is a market with a few dominant firms producing identical or closely substituted products whose contribution is not negligible, making the firms mutually interdependent. Entry is hard because of economies of scale, large capital requirements, patents and raw material control, and the duopoly is its simplest two-firm case. Oligopolists are price makers with downward-sloping AR curves and MR below AR, but their demand curves keep shifting as rivals react to each other's price changes.
